name: Automated Lead Generation
desc: Automated Reddit lead generation system that monitors hiring posts, classifies them with LLMs, and sends relevant leads straight to Discord.
challenge: The main hurdle with building an automated lead generation system with Reddit was its API. Around 2023, Reddit introduced restrictions that made frequent API access difficult, while rate limits were a constant concern. RSS feeds provided a way to monitor posts without depending entirely on the API, but they were slower and still needed to be polled carefully. I needed a system that could work around these limitations while staying lightweight enough to run continuously in the background.
approach: My main focus with this project was working around Reddit's API restrictions without sacrificing how quickly new leads could be detected. I used RSS feeds as the primary source and built smart polling that adjusts request intervals based on subreddit activity and rate limits. Posts then pass through multiple filters before reaching an LLM, which decides whether they are actually hiring leads. Once a lead is found, Discord was used as the delivery layer because it follows a simple one-click philosophy: receive the lead, open it, and take action.

metrics.label: Background Monitoring
metrics.sub: Continuously monitors Reddit feeds for potential hiring posts

metrics.label: Lead Outreach
metrics.sub: Relevant leads are delivered directly through Discord for quick action

metrics.label: Lead Filtering
metrics.sub: Local filtering and LLM classification reduce unnecessary inference requests

process.title: Discovery
process.desc: The Reddit API had restrictions imposed around mid-2023, making frequent polling difficult and turning rate limits into a real engineering concern. I looked for another way to monitor posts and settled on RSS feeds. They were slower, but they gave me a workable source that I could build around. I also wanted the final workflow to follow a simple one-click outreach philosophy.

process.title: Design
process.desc: To work around the slower RSS feeds and rate limits, I built smart polling that changes how frequently each subreddit is checked based on its activity. A multi-layered filtering system was added so obvious non-leads could be dropped before reaching an LLM. I also made the ingestion process asynchronous and chose Discord as the notification layer because it keeps the final interaction simple.

process.title: Implementation
process.desc: Each subreddit is monitored through its RSS feed and polled according to its activity. Async background workers keep the ingestion process from blocking while the filtering pipeline first checks posts locally and then uses an LLM when deeper classification is needed. Multiple LLM providers can be used as fallbacks, while captured posts are stored for later inspection and analysis.

outcome: The project was a great learning opportunity because it forced me to solve real-world problems under real constraints. I had to work around Reddit's API restrictions, deal with slower RSS feeds, manage rate limits, and still keep the system responsive. The result runs 24/7 with minimal overhead, classifies incoming posts automatically, and notifies me through Discord so I can act on a lead in one click. The system also preserves posts, which lets me study the market and gather inspiration for writing self-introductions and outreach.

features.label: Adaptive Smart Polling
features.desc: dynamic RSS polling intervals adjust based on subreddit activity and rate limits
features.detail: Each subreddit is polled according to how active its feed is. The system can increase or decrease polling frequency instead of repeatedly making requests at a fixed interval, reducing unnecessary traffic while keeping active feeds responsive.

features.label: Pluggable LLM Classification
features.desc: multiple LLM providers can classify whether a post is a genuine hiring lead
features.detail: Posts that survive the initial filters are passed to an LLM for deeper classification. The provider layer supports different inference backends, making it possible to switch between hosted models and local models without changing the rest of the pipeline.

features.label: Multi-Layered Filtering
features.desc: local filtering removes obvious non-leads before using LLM inference
features.detail: The pipeline does not send every Reddit post to an LLM. Local rules first remove posts that clearly do not match the requirements, reducing unnecessary inference requests before the more expensive classification step.

features.label: Passive Post Ingestion
features.desc: non-blocking background workers continuously capture incoming posts
features.detail: Posts are continuously collected in the background without requiring manual interaction. The ingestion pipeline stores relevant data and keeps the monitoring process separate from the notification and classification stages.

features.label: Database Debug & Developer Tools
features.desc: built-in tools for inspecting leads, querying data, and managing the database
features.detail: Developer tooling makes it easier to inspect captured posts, review classification results, run queries, and debug the pipeline without having to manually work through the database.

features.label: Provider Fallback & Rate-Limit Handling
features.desc: automatically handles provider failures and rate limits across multiple backends
features.detail: The system can react to provider failures, rate limits, and network issues by switching to another available inference backend instead of allowing a single provider failure to stop the entire pipeline.

name: CRSOM
desc: The first digital solution for BZU's CRSOM event, built around a complex registration system, tournament-specific rules, and automated data handling.
challenge: The main challenge was figuring out how to turn CRSOM's tournament rules into a registration system that could actually handle them. Each game had different player limits and requirements, while registrations could include multiple students and mentors. The form also needed to handle dynamic fees, image uploads, validation, and updates without becoming confusing for the person filling it out.
approach: With only 7 days to build the entire solution, I focused on making the registration flow reliable before adding anything unnecessary. I worked through the tournament rules, built dynamic player and mentor fields, added fee calculations and validation, and connected everything to a REST API. I also added image compression and detailed error handling so users could understand what went wrong instead of being left with raw backend errors.

metrics.label: Students Registered
metrics.sub: Through a single digital registration platform

metrics.label: Digital Solution for CRSOM
metrics.sub: The event's first complete digital registration system

process.title: Discovery
process.desc: I first worked with the BZU event organizers to understand how the event worked, what information they needed, and how the tournament rules affected registration. The design also changed frequently as they refined what they wanted, so I had to keep the implementation flexible.

process.title: Design
process.desc: I designed the registration flow around the organizers' requirements rather than forcing the rules into a generic form. The biggest challenge was making a large, data-heavy form usable on mobile while still supporting dynamic students, mentors, games, fees, and validation.

process.title: Implementation
process.desc: I built the frontend and connected it to a REST API with validation and error handling throughout the registration flow. Tournament rules were enforced before submission, duplicate entries were checked against the database, and registration data was exposed through an automated export pipeline for the organizers.

outcome: CRSOM became the event's first digital registration solution, with more than 300 students registering through the platform. Building the whole system in just 7 days forced me to work quickly without cutting corners on reliability. More importantly, it taught me how to turn unusual business rules into a working system, especially when the requirements did not fit the usual structure of a registration form.

features.label: Dynamic Complex Forms
features.desc: registration forms that adapt to the selected games, students, mentors, and other requirements
features.detail: The form dynamically creates and validates student and mentor fields based on the user's selections. This allowed different registration scenarios to be handled without creating separate forms for every case.

features.label: Automated Data Export
features.desc: structured registration data exposed for spreadsheet and admin workflows
features.detail: I built a dedicated backend route that formats registration data into a structure that could be consumed by external spreadsheet and administrative tools, reducing the need to manually process submissions.

features.label: Tournament Rule Validation
features.desc: game-specific player limits and team requirements enforced before submission
features.detail: The validation layer handles rules that differ between games, including exact player combinations and maximum team sizes. This keeps invalid registrations from reaching the database.

features.label: Duplicate Registration Protection
features.desc: database checks prevent duplicate participants and submissions
features.detail: The system checks important registration fields against existing records, including student and teacher contact information, CNICs, and user identifiers, before accepting a submission.

features.label: Human-Readable Errors
features.desc: raw validation errors converted into messages users can actually understand
features.detail: I built a custom error parser that converts backend and Joi validation errors into readable messages, including correctly identifying which student or mentor field needs attention.

name: Twitter REST API
desc: Twitter-like REST API focused on scalable backend architecture, asynchronous background processing, and fast data access through Redis caching.
challenge: I wanted to create something more than a basic Twitter clone. The main challenge was designing the architecture behind a large REST API while keeping it fast and responsive. It needed to handle frequent operations such as fetching tweets and view counts without repeatedly hitting the database. The system also needed background processing for tasks that did not need to block API requests.
approach: My main focus with this project was the backend architecture rather than simply adding endpoints. I used Redis as a caching layer so frequently requested data could be returned without querying PostgreSQL every time. Celery handles background processes such as syncing view counts from the cache back into the database, keeping those operations away from the main request cycle.

metrics.label: Non critical tasks offloaded
metrics.sub: Using celery non critical tasks such as views counting were cached and scheduled for later

metrics.label: Reduced DB operations.
metrics.sub: By implementing caching (Redis) many request hit cache instead of the DB.

metrics.label: API enpoints
metrics.sub: Structered for 6 core domains (Auth, Users, Tweets, Replies, Lists, Bookmarks).

process.title: Architecture
process.desc: I first broke the application into its main resources: users, tweets, replies, bookmarks, and lists. Each resource needed its own CRUD operations where appropriate, while authentication was kept separate. The goal was to make the API large without making the architecture difficult to maintain.

process.title: Performance
process.desc: A Twitter-like application constantly reads data, so hitting PostgreSQL for every request would create unnecessary overhead. I added Redis as a caching layer and designed the API to return cached data when available. Celery was then introduced for operations that could safely happen in the background.

process.title: Implementation
process.desc: I implemented more than 36 endpoints across the main API resources, backed by PostgreSQL. Redis handles frequently accessed data while Celery processes background jobs such as syncing cached view counts into the database. The result is an API where the request cycle stays focused on returning a response instead of doing every operation synchronously.

outcome: This project taught me how much of backend development is really about architecture. Building the endpoints was only one part of it. I had to think about where data should live, when it should be cached, and which operations should happen outside the request cycle. The final API has more than 36 endpoints, uses Redis for fast reads, PostgreSQL as the primary database, and Celery for background processing.

features.label: Celery Background Processing
features.desc: background workers handle operations that do not need to block API responses
features.detail: Celery workers process asynchronous tasks such as syncing tweet view counts from Redis back into PostgreSQL, keeping slower operations outside the main request cycle.

features.label: Built-In Redis Caching
features.desc: cached results are returned directly when available
features.detail: The API checks Redis before querying PostgreSQL for cacheable data. This reduces repeated database reads and keeps frequently accessed resources fast.

features.label: Resource-Based REST API
features.desc: 36+ endpoints organized around the application's core resources
features.detail: The API is structured around authentication, users, tweets, replies, bookmarks, and lists, with CRUD operations where they make sense for each resource.

features.label: Tweet & Reply System
features.desc: complete API support for creating and managing tweets and replies
features.detail: Tweet and reply resources support the operations required to create, retrieve, update, and delete content while keeping their relationships manageable through the API.

features.label: Bookmark Management
features.desc: lightweight bookmark creation and removal without unnecessary CRUD operations
features.detail: Bookmarks use a focused resource design where only the operations that make sense for the feature are exposed instead of forcing a generic CRUD structure.

features.label: List Management
features.desc: full CRUD support for user-created Twitter-style lists
features.detail: Users can create, retrieve, update, and delete lists through dedicated API endpoints, with the architecture leaving room for managing list membership separately.

name: Dotfiles
desc: Modular Arch Linux configuration built around GNU tools, custom window management, a tailored development environment, and lightweight system automation.
challenge: The main challenge with maintaining a Linux setup is keeping everything consistent without turning the configuration into a collection of random tweaks. I wanted the system to stay modular, easy to understand, and lightweight. Every part of the desktop had to serve a purpose, while custom scripts and services needed to work together without adding unnecessary overhead.
approach: My main focus with this project was the architecture of the system rather than its appearance. I chose GNU tools because of their simplicity and modularity, then structured the configuration so individual components could be changed without affecting the rest of the setup. Hyprland handles the current Wayland desktop while my previous Qtile and X11 configuration is still maintained. Around it, I built a consistent development workflow, custom utilities, and lightweight desktop services.

metrics.label: Idle CPU Reduction
metrics.sub: Optimized moving wallpapers from roughly 20% idle CPU usage to 10%

metrics.label: Display Architectures
metrics.sub: Maintains both the current Wayland setup and previous X11 configuration

metrics.label: Custom Workflow
metrics.sub: Development, desktop, browser, and system utilities configured around a single workflow

process.title: Architecture
process.desc: I started with modularity as the main principle. GNU utilities made it easy to keep individual pieces of the system separate and predictable. Instead of relying on one large configuration, each component has its own configuration and can be changed independently.

process.title: Desktop
process.desc: The desktop evolved from Qtile and X11 into my current Hyprland and Wayland setup. I configured Waybar, Rofi, and SwayNC around the workflow I actually use, including a custom Rofi theme and notification setup. The older X11 configuration remains available rather than being discarded.

process.title: Optimization
process.desc: System scripts handle repetitive tasks such as Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, screenshots, and window capture. I also experimented with moving wallpapers, but the initial version used too much CPU while idle. I slowed and simplified the rendering until I found a version that kept the effect without wasting resources, cutting idle CPU usage from around 20% to 10%.

outcome: This project became less about customizing Linux and more about designing a system that behaves exactly how I expect it to. The configuration is modular, portable, and easy to modify when my workflow changes. My development environment, desktop, browser, and system utilities all follow the same philosophy: keep things simple, remove unnecessary overhead, and automate the repetitive parts.

features.label: Modular Configuration Architecture
features.desc: separate system configurations built around simple, composable GNU tools
features.detail: The dotfiles are organized by application and responsibility, allowing individual components to be changed, replaced, or restored without restructuring the entire system.

features.label: Wayland Desktop Environment
features.desc: Hyprland setup with custom window management, notifications, panels, and application launcher
features.detail: Hyprland provides the current window management layer, with Waybar, Rofi, and SwayNC configured to fit the same workflow. Previous Qtile and X11 configurations are also preserved.

features.label: Integrated Development Workflow
features.desc: Neovim and terminal tooling configured around a consistent development workflow
features.detail: Neovim was configured from scratch with custom keybindings, language tooling, navigation, completion, formatting, and project workflows. Tmux provides persistent multi-terminal sessions without relying on a graphical terminal layout.

features.label: System Automation Scripts
features.desc: small shell utilities for common desktop and system operations
features.detail: Custom scripts simplify Wi-Fi and Bluetooth control, screenshots, window capture, and screen selection. Repetitive system actions become single commands instead of manual sequences.

features.label: Performance-Focused Desktop
features.desc: system effects tuned around resource usage rather than visual effects alone
features.detail: Moving wallpapers were initially too expensive to run continuously, consuming around 20% CPU while idle. The rendering speed and workload were reduced until the same idea could run at roughly half the idle CPU usage.

features.label: Minimal Browser Environment
features.desc: Firefox interface redesigned around a clean and distraction-free workflow
features.detail: Custom userChrome.css and userContent.css configurations control the browser's interface and page presentation, keeping Firefox visually consistent with the rest of the desktop.
